k978: On 26 November 2019 an M6.4 earthquake struck with its epicentre near Durrës. 51 people died, more than 14,000 buildings were damaged and 2,500 were left uninhabitable; the damage exceeded €1 billion. Hotels and homes collapsed in Plazh and Shkëmbi i Kavajës in particular. Reconstruction cost more than €1 billion and ran on a fast track that drew accusations of favouritism, and four years later about 2,500 families were still without permanent housing.
k979: What it did to the market
k980: Since then Durrës has had two markets under one address. New buildings carry a lasting premium — buyers pay for confidence in the structure — and older stock trades at a discount or stands still. Most apartments on the beach strip are more than 30 years old, and the top prices you see quoted apply to a small share of new units.
k981: The gap is widest in Shkëmbi i Kavajës: new builds ask €1,200–2,000/m², older flats €450–800/m². In Plazh the second line, mostly older stock, has traded far below new first-line units. Shkozet and old Plazh are where the discount on old buildings is most visible.
k982: The ground is part of the picture too. The Durrës coast is sandy, and settlement has been confirmed even in brand-new towers at the Durrës marina — so a recent construction year alone is not a guarantee either.
k983: How to check an older building
k984: <s0>Construction year.</s0> Our working rule for Durrës is a building from 2020 or later, or an independent seismic assessment of an older one. Ask for the year in writing.
k985: <s0>Post-earthquake assessment.</s0> Ask whether the building was inspected after November 2019, what category it was given and whether any repairs were made. No paperwork is an answer too.
k986: <s0>Floors against the permit.</s0> Count the floors and compare them with the building permit. Extra floors added without permission are common on this coast, load the structure beyond its design and can cloud the title.
k987: <s0>Ownership extract.</s0> Pull the ownership certificate (kartela e pasurisë) from the cadastre ASHK yourself: it shows the owner and any encumbrances. An occupancy permit (leje përdorimi) should exist for the building.
k988: <s0>An engineer, not an agent.</s0> Pay an independent structural engineer to look at cracks, the stairwell, the ground floor and the roof. It costs little against the price gap.
k989: <s0>Budget.</s0> A full standard renovation costs about €200–300/m² in Albania, mid-range €300–400/m², before windows, kitchen and appliances. Structural strengthening is a separate budget.
k990: <s0>Insurance.</s0> Home insurance covering earthquake costs roughly €1 per m² a year — cheap, but check what the policy requires of the building.
k991: When an older flat is still the right buy
k992: An older flat makes sense for a buyer who plans to live in it or let it long-term, has budgeted the renovation, and has an engineer's report in hand — especially in the centre, where the city holds its value year-round. It makes least sense as a quick short-let buy on the strip that the earthquake hit hardest.

k1010: Reference Prices in Durrës in 2026: What Applies, What Was Only Proposed, and What It Means When You Buy
k1011: If you have read that Durrës reference prices tripled on 1 January 2026, that is not what happened. The Ministry of Finance published a new map in July 2025, with the port zone at 200,000 lek per square metre, for use from 1 January 2026. It was never approved. The government reopened the review, and in July 2026 Durrës was still using the values of 2016. For a buyer the difference matters less than the headlines suggest — but it matters in three specific places.
k1013: Albania keeps an official price per square metre for property in each area — the reference price, or çmimi i referencës. It is not a valuation of your flat. It is a floor: notary fees and taxes are calculated on the contract price or on the reference price times the area, whichever is higher. It also sets the fiscal value used for the annual property tax.
k1015: As of July 2026, districts outside Tirana still apply the reference values set in 2016, and Durrës has one rate for the whole city rather than zones. Recent reporting puts it at 67,500 lek/m², about €730 — while some compilations list 71,200 lek/m² under the 2023 instruction. Ask the notary which figure applies to your address; it is the notary who calculates the fees.
k1016: Either way, the rate is far below what Durrës actually costs. Apartments ask about €1,200–1,700/m² in Plazh and €1,900–2,800/m² in the centre, so on an ordinary purchase your contract price is already above the reference, and the reference changes nothing about your fees.
k1017: What was proposed — and why it stalled
k1018: The July 2025 draft split Durrës into 13 cadastral zones, from 45,000 to 200,000 lek/m². The port and marina zone would have gone from 67,500 to 200,000 lek/m², an increase of about 196%; other zones were set at 140,000, 124,000, 100,000 and 45,000. A later proposal for villages put Gjiri i Lalzit and Hamallaj at 190,000 lek/m², the highest rural figure in the country. A local expert noted at the time that a rate of about €2,000/m² in Plazh would realistically match only around 5% of the housing there.
k1019: The draft was published for consultation and never approved. In 2026 the government sent it back to a working group with a deadline of 20 April. By June the finance minister was saying the work was still under way and more complex than expected because it involves the municipalities, and in July coastal zones were reported as still on hold while their market prices were checked again.
k1021: <s0>Notary fees and the transfer tax.</s0> The notary charges about 0.35% on sales between 100,000 and 6 million lek, falling in steps for larger amounts, calculated on the higher of the contract price and the reference value. The same rule sets the base for the 2% transfer tax. With today's single rate, the contract price almost always decides.
k1022: <s0>Capital gains when you sell.</s0> Capital gains tax is 15% of the difference between your sale and purchase price, and the sale price used is the higher of the actual price and the reference value. A new, higher map would raise that floor for resales in the dearest zones. It also means that an understated purchase price in your own contract becomes a larger taxable gain later.
k1023: <s0>The annual property tax.</s0> Housing is taxed at 0.05% of its fiscal value — reference price times area — and municipalities can move that by 30% either way. On a 60 m² flat that is about 2,025 lek a year at 67,500 lek/m²; at the proposed 200,000 it would be 6,000 lek. Noticeable, but small.
k1025: Until 31 December 2026, any owner can revalue a property to its market value by applying to the cadastre ASHK and paying 5% on the difference, instead of paying 15% capital gains tax on it at a later sale. Payment is due by 31 March 2027. For flats the value is reduced by 1% for each year of use. If you already own in Durrës and expect to sell in the next few years, it is worth asking a tax adviser whether it pays off in your case.
k1026: What to do as a buyer
k1027: Put the real price in the contract. It protects you on resale and costs little in fees.
k1028: Ask the notary for the reference value of the exact address before you agree the final price.
k1029: Don't accept a seller's argument that "the new reference prices" justify a higher price — they are not in force.
k1030: Check the status again before you sell or revalue: the map can still be approved.

k1048: Golem's Sewage Problem: What It Means If You Buy an Apartment There
k1049: Golem has a sewage problem, and nobody selling apartments there mentions it. Discharges onto the beach have been documented again and again, and the World Bank-backed project meant to fix the network is unfinished. It has not stopped prices rising. What it changes is how you should plan to use the flat, how much rent you can count on, and what you need to see with your own eyes before you sign.
k1051: Albanian media have reported sewage flooding onto Golem beach repeatedly, and in our research Golem ranks among the dirtiest beaches of the Durrës coast. The fix — a sewerage project supported by the World Bank — has not been completed. Neither Durrës nor Golem has a Blue Flag beach; in 2026 the only Blue Flag beach in Albania is at Palasë, in the south.
k1052: Golem is also administratively part of Kavajë municipality, not Durrës, even though the market treats it as the Durrës coast. That matters for the utility you deal with — water and sewerage in the Golem/Kavajë unit are billed at 50 lek/m³ for water, 30 lek/m³ for sewerage and a 200 lek monthly fee — and for the municipality that issues and enforces building permits.
k1053: What it has — and hasn't — done to prices
k1054: So far, nothing visible. The second and third line ask €1,100–1,500/m² and are rising 8–15% a year. The first line, where almost nothing new is being built, asks €2,000–2,500/m². Demand comes mainly from buyers from Kosovo, the Albanian diaspora and short-let investors, and it keeps growing regardless.
k1055: The effect shows up in the rental calendar instead. Golem is a pure summer market: occupancy for short lets peaks at about 55% in August and drops to about 13% in January, and around 27% of the listings there already ask for 30-night minimum stays. On a second- or third-line flat bought for €60,000–97,500, we estimate €4,000–7,000 a year in rent, a gross yield of 5–8% — with the environment as a risk on top.
